title: “Overachievers” and the Tyranny of Low Expectations
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a student asking panelists what motivated them to overachieve, Stuart argues that the culture's definition of overachiever, someone who simply does a student's work, reflects a tyranny of low expectations that adults often reinforce. Belonging to a class is not enough unless students belong to something worthwhile, here a countercultural community in which personal achievement is normal. His first step is helping students see the absurdity of the word, since achievement means realizing one's potential and cannot be exceeded. His second is building a classroom culture where achievement is the norm, through mantras like do hard things, concrete requirements in student work, and repeated contrast with the dominant culture. The piece is a culture-building argument about what students belong to.
points: Many adults set expectations as a list of don'ts, so ordinary effort is treated as overachieving.
Belonging only motivates if the community students join values achievement, which requires a deliberately countercultural classroom.
The reframe from overachiever to achiever asks what is the best I am capable of here, grounding effort in human potential rather than competition.
Culture is built through mantras, concrete work requirements and repeated contrasts with the dominant culture.
quotes: Many adults reinforce this when their chief expectations for teenagers are that they DON’T: don’t fail classes, don’t cyberbully or sext, don’t do drugs. Avoid self-destruction, and you’re great. Everything above that, like making your bed and stuff, is overachieving.

Belonging alone doesn’t do much unless we can answer a second question — belonging to what? And the answer has to be to a countercultural community, a group of people for whom personal achievement is normal and worthy.

Overachievers definitionally do MORE than achievement (the realization of our potential) requires. - What is the best I am capable of in this class? - What is the most I am capable of growing, learning, becoming this semester in here?

Achievers are en route to flourishing lives. Achievers are what I want my children to be, both the little ones in my home and the teenagers I teach. I want my kids to be people who push themselves, who make time six days a week for studying (even in hard home life situations), who refuse to believe that they can’t succeed in math or history or literature or physical education — not because I want my kids to be The Best or to Compete in the Real World, but because I believe in the realization of human potential.

The second step, then — once we’ve helped our students see the absurdity of the dominant culture’s definition of “overachievement” — is to create classroom cultures where achievers are the norm. Achievement is what we do here.
